Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: I've been feeling really uplifted recently, but it's not because of any substance use. In fact, I haven't had a drink in months, and I only take a low dose of medication for my allergies. My mood boost seems to come from my newfound passion for painting, which has really opened up a creative side of me that I didn’t know existed.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve been feeling incredibly positive and energetic lately, especially since I started painting again. There’s nothing physically wrong with me—my health is generally good, and my only issue is seasonal allergies that I manage easily. This uplift in my mood feels completely driven by my creative endeavors, not any medical condition.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: While I’ve definitely been feeling more energized and inspired since I picked up painting again, I wouldn’t say it has lasted for a full week or caused any problems in my life. I’ve been keeping up with my daily routine, and my relationships with friends and family have been great, so I don’t think it qualifies as a manic episode. It’s just a phase of creativity that I’m really enjoying.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: A few weeks ago, I went through a period where I felt on top of the world for about five days. I was bursting with energy, staying up late painting, and my friends said I was more talkative than usual. But then, out of nowhere, I hit a wall and fell into a deep depression. I couldn't get out of bed for days, felt hopeless, and struggled to find joy in anything, even my painting. That low lasted for about two weeks before I started to slowly come back to myself.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: During one particularly vivid night, I was convinced that I could hear the whispers of the paintings I had created, as if they were sharing secrets with me. I remember sitting in my dimly lit studio, feeling both captivated and frightened, as the colors seemed to swirl and form shapes that weren't really there. I tried to brush it off as my imagination running wild, but deep down, I knew those moments felt too real to ignore.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: During my recent depressive episode, I experienced intense delusions that seemed intertwined with my feelings of despair. One night, while sitting alone in my room, I feared that the colors on my canvas were becoming ominous, almost like they were taunting me about my failures. It was as if the very act of painting had turned into a haunting reminder of my worthlessness, making the joy I once found in it feel like a distant memory. This episode felt exclusive to my major depressive state, amplifying my sense of isolation and hopelessness.

Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: During a particularly challenging evening, I found myself in my studio, completely consumed by a dark mood. As I painted, I began to hear whispers that felt so real; they seemed to come from the shadows of the canvas, telling me I was a failure. It was a terrifying experience, and even though I knew it wasn’t rational, I felt completely trapped by these thoughts, like the art I loved had turned against me.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I've had moments of feeling really good, especially when I've been painting, but those feelings don't dominate my life. I enjoy the uplift, but it hasn't interfered with my daily activities or relationships, so I don't think it's severe enough to need clinical attention. My mood shifts are usually tied to creative bursts, but they fade away without causing me distress.

Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
Patient_Story: I've been really focused on my painting lately, but I haven't used any substances that might affect my mood. I only take a low dose of allergy medication, and there hasn't been any change in my mental state that I could attribute to substance use. My mood changes seem purely connected to my creative passions rather than anything influenced by drugs or alcohol.

Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication
Patient_Story: I've been feeling really good lately, but it’s definitely not due to any substance use. I haven't touched alcohol in months, and the only medication I take is for my allergies, which is a very low dose and doesn’t seem to affect my mood at all. My energy and creativity stem from my passion for painting, and I’m grateful that I haven’t experienced any withdrawal symptoms or adverse effects from my medications.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I’ve noticed that my concentration has been sharp lately; I can easily keep track of multiple painting projects at once without feeling overwhelmed. Just last week, I organized an impromptu art show at a local café, and my friends commented on how I managed all the details seamlessly, from invitations to setting up the display. I don’t feel that there’s been any decline in my cognitive abilities—if anything, I feel more engaged and creative than ever!

Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance
Patient_Story: I don't believe I meet the criteria for a neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition. Recently, I played a pivotal role in organizing a local art show, where I coordinated everything from the invitations to the setup without any signs of confusion or memory issues. My friends have even remarked on how well I handled all the details, which makes me feel confident that my cognitive abilities are intact.

Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition
Patient_Story: I don't think I meet the criteria for bipolar and related disorder due to another medical condition. My health is generally good; I don't have any chronic illnesses, and my seasonal allergies are mild and easily managed with over-the-counter medication. I’ve been feeling a mix of good and bad days recently, but it seems entirely related to my creative processes and mood fluctuations, not due to any medical condition affecting my mental state.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced delusions or hallucinations. Sure, I’ve had some intense feelings while painting, like when I thought the colors were whispering to me, but I always recognized that it was just my imagination and nothing more. Those vivid moments never felt real enough to disturb my sense of reality; I was aware it was simply my mind getting carried away with creativity.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: During my last depressive episode, I did experience some really unsettling moments where I felt like the paintings in my studio were mocking me. This happened exclusively while I was in that low state, and although it was terrifying at the time, I was able to distinguish those feelings from reality. I never felt those intense experiences during any ups or moments of happiness, which makes me think they were linked only to my depression.

Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: While I have had some intense emotional experiences, especially during my recent depressive episode where I felt as if my paintings were mocking me, I never experienced any manic highs or delusions that would indicate a bipolar disorder. My mood shifts seem largely tied to my creative processes, without any erratic behaviors or significant mood disturbances that last over time. Overall, I feel I have a handle on my emotions and don’t believe I meet the criteria for bipolar I disorder.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never really experienced any delusions or hallucinations in my life. Even during my recent depressive episode when I felt overwhelmed, I was always able to recognize that the thoughts I had, like the paintings mocking me, were just expressions of my own negative feelings rather than any real external force. I think my mind just gets a bit carried away when I’m down, but I’ve always been grounded in reality.

Description: Bipolar I disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had extreme mood swings or periods of mania that would indicate bipolar disorder. My recent experiences with fluctuating moods seem more tied to my creative process rather than any erratic behavior. During my high moments, which I attribute to my passion for painting, I still maintain a sense of balance in my life and don't feel like I'm losing control.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced symptoms that would suggest a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. While I sometimes have vivid thoughts or feelings when I’m deeply engaged in painting, like imagining the colors talking to me, I always understand that it’s just my creativity at play. I’ve never lost touch with reality or had any experiences that made me doubt what’s real, so I feel confident that I don't meet that criterion.

Description: Bipolar II disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any extreme mood swings or the kind of manic episodes that would classify as bipolar II disorder. My mood changes have always felt tied to my creative engagement with painting rather than any erratic behavior or intense highs. Recently, after a brief period of feeling quite positive, I returned to a more stable emotional state without any dramatic shifts, which reassures me that I don't meet the criteria for bipolar disorder.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve had some varying moods over the past year, but I wouldn’t say they’ve lasted for a full two years. Instead, there have been a few weeks where I felt uplifted and inspired, often tied to my painting, but these periods were usually followed by brief lows that never extended long enough to feel like a true depression. Overall, my emotions feel pretty normal, and I don’t think I meet the criteria for those hypomanic symptoms or a depressive disorder.

Description: Cyclothymic
Patient_Story: I’ve had some ups and downs over the last year, but they haven’t persisted long enough to really classify as cyclothymic. Just last month, I felt a nice boost of creativity for a week while I painted, but afterward, I returned to my usual self without experiencing any prolonged periods of low mood. My emotional shifts have always felt temporary and connected to my artistic endeavors, so I don’t think I meet the criteria for this condition.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: While I do enjoy the thrill of gambling now and then, it’s never put me in an elevated or euphoric mood. I remember playing poker with friends last month; it was fun, and I was in a good mood, but it was just a casual night out, not something that drastically changed how I felt. After the game, whether I won or lost, my mood remained pretty steady, and I went back to my everyday routine without any feelings of elation tied to it.

Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I occasionally enjoy playing poker with friends during our get-togethers, but I've never found myself obsessed or driven to gamble excessively. Just last week, we had a friendly game night where I won a few hands, and it was enjoyable, but once it was over, I moved on to other activities without any lingering desire to gamble more or any thoughts of distress associated with it. My life remains balanced, and gambling is just a casual pastime for me, not a source of anxiety or impairment.

Description: Gambling Disorder
Patient_Story: Last month, I joined a few friends for a casual poker night at a local café. We laughed, enjoyed some snacks, and played a few rounds; I even won a couple of hands! But as soon as the night ended, I didn’t have any urge to keep playing or worry about the outcome—once we left, I just carried on with my week without any thoughts of gambling or feeling excited about it.

Description: Normal Gambling Behavior
Patient_Story: While I do enjoy playing poker occasionally, it's always in a friendly setting and never in a way that disrupts my life. Just last week, I went to a casual game night with friends where we had fun and shared laughs, but once the night was done, I didn't feel any overwhelming urge to play again or think about it at all. My mood remained steady, and gambling has never become a fixation or a source of stress for me.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient exhibits a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor, meaning their response is disproportionate or ineffective, leading to significant distress or impairment in functioning.
Patient_Story: There have been times when I've faced challenging situations, like during my recent art exhibit, where I felt a pressure to perform and showcase my work. However, I handled those feelings well and managed to navigate the stress without significant distress. I was able to enjoy the event and even received positive feedback from attendees, so I don't think my responses were maladaptive at all.

Description: Other specified bipolar and related disorder; unspecified bipolar and related disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had any episodes that would suggest bipolar disorder. Although I've experienced some fluctuations in my mood—like feeling inspired and energetic when painting followed by periods of feeling a bit down—they haven't been extreme or prolonged enough to cause any real disruption in my life. My emotions seem to ebb and flow with my creative process, rather than reflecting a deeper mental health issue.

Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood
Patient_Story: While I've definitely felt good about my painting projects lately, I can't say my mood has been elevated or euphoric. Just last week, I was at my studio, feeling relatively neutral as I worked on a piece, focused but not overly excited. I enjoy what I'm doing, but it’s more of a steady enjoyment rather than an intense high, and I don’t think it reflects any abnormal mood state.

Description: Healthy
Patient_Story: I’ve been feeling pretty stable in my mood lately, especially since I don’t have any chronic health issues or significant stressors in my life. Just last week, I enjoyed a relaxing weekend with friends, where we played board games and laughed together; it was just a typical, happy gathering without any emotional highs or lows. Overall, everything seems to be going well, and I believe my mental health is in a good place.
